strengths: Novel uncertainty decomposition framework for MAD providing fresh theoretical perspective on debate dynamics and why debates succeed or fail
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (MATH, GSM8K, AMC, AIME) with both homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations
Well-motivated problem addressing real challenges in MAD including sycophancy, token entropy increases, and performance divergence
Honest treatment of limitations and acknowledgment of theoretical assumptions (ensemble proxy, NLL as AU proxy)
Practical algorithmic contribution with interpretable mechanisms (epistemic influence rewards, aleatoric uncertainty weighting)
weaknesses: Critical theoretical gap: System-level uncertainty decomposition (Prop 3.2) relies on unjustified ensemble-of-experts proxy assuming agent distributions are exchangeable posterior samples, which is false for correlated debate contexts; no approximation error analysis provided

Fundamental issue with aleatoric uncertainty definition in deterministic domains: Paper redefines AU as 'LLM decoding randomness' rather than task uncertainty, conflating model miscalibration with true aleatoric uncertainty; token-level NLL acknowledged as imperfect proxy for semantic uncertainty

Theorem 3.3 on heterogeneous epistemic gain is tautological: assumes the heterogeneous novelty condition that should be proven; proof merely applies chain rule with no characterization of when condition holds or empirical validation
Modest experimental improvements (5-7% for heterogeneous, 1-2% for homogeneous) without statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; gains potentially within noise

Missing critical baselines and comparisons: No evaluation against concurrent MARL methods (MAPoRL, MARFT, MAGRPO, AT-GRPO) mentioned in related work; only vanilla IPPO baseline makes it unclear whether gains come from proposed mechanisms or implementation differences

Protocol deviation undermines evaluation: Removes aggregation (majority voting) to focus on individual agents, but MAD is deployed with aggregation; single-agent accuracy metric doesn't capture real-world debate benefits shown in Figure 1

Insufficient technical detail and reproducibility gaps: Epistemic reward calculation via ΔR_peer is vague; trajectory-level rollout strategy (K=16 then K=1) lacks justification; answer semantic equivalence merging underdeveloped
Limited scope reducing generalizability: Only math reasoning domain tested; primarily Qwen models; only N=2 agents; no scaling experiments; no cross-model-family evaluation
Hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary: α_au=0.25, η=0.25 lack justification or ablation; exponential weighting W(U_i)=exp(-α_au·U_i) not motivated

strengths: Novel perspective on MAD through epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty decomposition
Systematic empirical analysis with effective visualizations of uncertainty dynamics across debate trajectories
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and model configurations
Honest acknowledgment of theoretical limitations (ensemble proxy, token-level NLL as uncertainty proxy)
weaknesses: Core theoretical framework relies on unvalidated assumption that LLMs perform implicit Bayesian reasoning over latent beliefs φᵢ; ensemble-of-experts proxy approximation never empirically verified
Modest and statistically unvalidated empirical improvements: homogeneous setting shows <1-2% gains (within noise), heterogeneous ~6% at T=5, no confidence intervals or significance tests provided

Disconnect between theory and algorithm: UMAD design choices (exponential weighting, intrinsic reward formulation) don't cleanly operationalize theoretical insights about epistemic gain Gepi(m) = I(φ; m|x, c)
Missing critical comparisons: no evaluation against recent MARL methods for MAD (MAPoRL, MARFT, AT-GRPO) mentioned in related work

Generalization concerns: limited to math reasoning on 3B-4B models; removal of aggregation stage makes results non-comparable to standard MAD evaluation; training on T=2 tested on T=5 doesn't isolate learning of debate behavior
Key theoretical assumption unverified: Theorem 3.3's 'heterogeneous novelty condition' I(φ; m_hetero|x,c,m_homo) ≥ I(φ; m'_homo|x,c,m_homo) is assumed but never empirically validated

Aleatoric uncertainty definition conflates concepts: for deterministic math problems, defining AU as 'decoding randomness' and using token-level NLL as proxy is questionable; unclear why decoding noise control optimizes reasoning
No statistical significance testing: improvements often within noise margins; sample sizes not clearly stated; no confidence intervals or error bars

Incomplete ablations: no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters (α_au, η, β); no justification for functional form choices (e.g., exponential weighting); insufficient isolation of component contributions

strengths: Novel Bayesian uncertainty decomposition framework for MAD that identifies the epistemic-aleatoric trade-off as key to debate effectiveness
Well-motivated problem addressing recent findings about MAD limitations in homogeneous settings
Comprehensive empirical analysis across homogeneous/heterogeneous settings with clear uncertainty dynamics visualization
Practical algorithm (UMAD) with meaningful improvements in heterogeneous debate (14% gain on MATH500)
Strong generalization from short-horizon training (T=2) to long-horizon evaluation (T=5) without divergence
Thorough experimental documentation including hyperparameters, prompts, and concrete debate examples
Theoretical contributions (Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.3) provide new perspective on why heterogeneous debate outperforms homogeneous
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: latent beliefs φ are theoretically central but computationally intractable; answer-level ensemble approximation lacks rigorous justification for posterior validity

Aleatoric uncertainty definition conflates decoding randomness with hallucination amplification, which should be epistemic (lack of knowledge); inconsistent use of token-level vs. answer-level entropy
Weak causality in epistemic influence reward (Eq. 5): attributing peer improvement to single agent's message without proper off-policy corrections or confounding factor analysis
Limited algorithmic novelty: confidence-aware advantage (Eq. 4) builds on Xie et al. 2025; GRPO extension follows recent MARL work (MAPoRL); main contribution is combining existing techniques

Incomplete ablations: no isolated evaluation of epistemic reward vs. aleatoric control; hyperparameter sensitivity (η=0.25, α_au=0.25) not analyzed; missing comparisons with concurrent MARL methods (MARFT, AT-GRPO)
Heterogeneous novelty condition in Theorem 3.3 assumes what it proves; lack of empirical validation that this condition actually holds in practice

Experimental scope limitations: only 3B-4B models tested; negligible improvements in homogeneous settings (0.4% on MATH500); 0% performance on AIME limits insights on hard problems; missing baseline comparisons with MAPoRL and other recent work
Unclear generalization: why does training with T=2 generalize to T=5? Is method learning robust debate or learning to ignore context after round 2? Limited to math reasoning domain.

strengths: Novel uncertainty decomposition framework providing genuine new insights into MAD failures through epistemic-aleatoric trade-off
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 7 models and 5 datasets with rigorous ablation studies isolating component contributions
Well-formulated theoretical analysis (Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.4) that elegantly characterizes belief updates and heterogeneous debate advantages
Consistent practical improvements showing robustness, particularly strong gains for weaker agents in heterogeneous settings (54.8→66.5 average accuracy)
Transparent discussion of limitations and honest treatment of gaps between theoretical motivation and operational proxies
Clear visualization and interpretation of uncertainty dynamics across different debate trajectories (Figure 2)
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: latent belief variable φ_i never directly estimated; ensemble-of-experts proxy lacks rigorous justification; token-level NLL as aleatoric proxy is pragmatic but imperfect with under-explored implications
Assumption 3.3 (Homogeneous Information Saturation) presented but never empirically validated or characterized for when it holds
Epistemic influence reward (Eq. 5) measures observable peer improvement rather than mutual information, creating loose connection to theoretical framework's information-theoretic motivation
Uncertainty measurement limited: K=16 samples may be insufficient for stable distribution estimation; common support set approach could artificially inflate disagreement; no sensitivity analysis

Restricted experimental scope: limited to verifiable math reasoning; only 2-agent teams tested; missing comparisons to recent uncertainty-aware debate methods; asymmetric improvements raise unclear question of whether gains reflect improved debate dynamics or easier weak-model teaching
Incomplete analysis: Figure 1's increasing entropy phenomenon under-explored; answer flip ratio analysis relegated to appendix; no characterization of failure modes or learned behavior changes
Statistical rigor concerns: no formal significance testing; some improvements overlap with error bars; inconsistent seed counts across experiments (5 vs. 3)

Modest improvements in homogeneous settings and saturation behavior suggest framework primarily effective when epistemic diversity exists; hyperparameter choices lack justification or sensitivity analysis

strengths: Well-motivated approach to analyzing MAD failures by removing aggregation and focusing on individual belief evolution; avoids confounding aggregation benefits with debate benefits
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across seven base models, multiple datasets (MATH, GSM8K, AMC, AIME), homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations, with ablations and answer-flipping analysis
Intuitive and computationally tractable operational framework using answer-level JSD decomposition (Proposition 3.2) that clearly correlates with debate success/failure patterns (Figure 2)
Substantial improvements in heterogeneous weaker-agent performance (54.8% → 66.5% average accuracy) with good generalization from 2-round training to 5-round inference
Honest treatment of limitations, acknowledging that uncertainty measures are operational proxies rather than exact Bayesian quantities; transparency about scope restrictions and future work
weaknesses: Significant gap between theoretical framework and practice: paper motivates analysis using latent beliefs φ_i but never works with them directly; jumps to answer-level distributions without rigorous justification that this approximates true belief updates

Critical training components are ad-hoc: token-level NLL used as aleatoric uncertainty proxy lacks validation it correlates with semantic instability; epistemic influence reward (Eq. 5) uses peer correctness improvement rather than true mutual information, potentially gameable

Limited practical scope of improvements: homogeneous debate (original MAD focus) shows only modest gains (~2-4%); heterogeneous gains primarily benefit weaker agent; unclear if improvements are from uncertainty decomposition or simply better GRPO training

Incremental theoretical contributions: Lemma 3.1 is trivial Bayes' rule reformulation; Proposition 3.2 is standard JSD decomposition; Theorem 3.4 formalizes obvious intuition about complementary evidence without deep insight

Restricted experimental scope: all evaluations on math with exact-match verification only; no experiments on open-ended tasks, code generation, or domains with ambiguous answers; scales linearly with N·T, limiting practical applicability

Incomplete baseline comparisons: no direct comparison with recent MAD variants (ReConcile, GroupDebate, DynaDebate); Single-GRPO baseline in appendix matches or exceeds UMAD on stronger agents; unclear if gains are from uncertainty guidance or training methodology

Answer-level distribution assumption unvalidated: claim that ensemble averages approximate Bayesian posteriors rests on 'mild assumption' (page 4) that is neither formalized nor empirically justified; conflates model averaging with true posterior inference

Unresolvedambiguity in failure modes: Figure 2f-l shows heterogeneous pairs failing despite high initial epistemic uncertainty; framework doesn't cleanly separate whether failures stem from 'aleatoric cost' or weaker model's limited reasoning ability

strengths: Novel uncertainty decomposition framework: epistemic (inter-agent disagreement) vs. aleatoric (within-agent instability) components provide operationally useful lens for diagnosing MAD failures
Strong theoretical contributions: Lemma 3.1 formalizes debate as Bayesian belief update; Theorem 3.4 explains heterogeneous advantage through conditional novelty rather than diversity alone
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5 datasets, 7 base models, homogeneous/heterogeneous configurations, thoughtful ablations demonstrating complementarity of uncertainty components
Consistent practical improvements: heterogeneous debate weaker agent improves from 54.8→66.5 average accuracy at T=5, generalizes from 2-round training to 5-round inference
Clear presentation: effective visualizations (Figures 2, 6) and logical flow from motivation through theory to empirics
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges gaps between theoretical concepts and operational proxies
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Epistemic/aleatoric uncertainties are operational proxies (answer-level JSD, token-level NLL) rather than true Bayesian quantities. Leap from latent beliefs φᵢ to answer distributions pᵢ,ₜ lacks rigor. Connection between theoretical G_epi (mutual information) and simple intrinsic reward (peer correctness improvement) is loose

Limited theoretical validation: Assumption 3.3 (homogeneous information saturation) is intuitive but never empirically verified. Pass@K interpretation may not hold when sampling diversity and semantic diversity diverge. Mixture model assumes exchangeable agents, violated in heterogeneous settings

Relatively simple RL algorithm: UMAD applies straightforward extensions (token-level weighting, peer improvement reward) to standard GRPO. Token weighting function W(U)=exp(-αU) lacks justification. Design choices (αau=0.25, η=0.25) are not ablated

Limited scope and applicability: Only N=2 agents; unclear scaling to larger teams. Restricted to math reasoning with verifiable answers; generalization to open-ended tasks unvalidated. Homogeneous debate shows only modest improvements, limiting applicability

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons to recent MAD methods (Li et al. 2026b, Zhu et al. 2026). Single-GRPO Pair achieves competitive performance on stronger agent (67.8 vs 65.8), questioning necessity of debate co-training
High variance in results: AIME tasks show ±5-8% standard deviations (Table 1), raising stability concerns. Large variability suggests instability of the approach or insufficient evaluation samples

Missing methodological details and ablations: No sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters. No exploration of alternative uncertainty proxies. Semantic uncertainty methods not compared. No ablation on K=16 sampling scale

Reproducibility concerns: Source code URL missing ('available at' incomplete). Prompt templates relegated to appendix. Some algorithmic choices (e.g., 'or select greedily' in Algorithm 1) leave ambiguity
